utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Before we continue with the evidence, one or two matters to deal with. First of all, it's plain to be seen that Judge Kwon is absent and will be detained for the rest of this week. So we will be sitting under the auspices of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Tieger, have you got an estimate for the time that's likely to take the Prosecution to examine in-chief? Last week it wasn't possible for you to give one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Mr. Robinson made the same inquiry in connection with preparation for cross-examination. I indicated to him that I considered that it was extremely likely that we would consume at least the full day today for examination-in-chief, and it was difficult to estimate beyond that. Again, that's just an estimate under the circumstances -- the best estimate under the circumstances but that's the information I provided him and the same information I would provide the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any observations as to that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, concerning the private session passages of General Smith's testimony, it would be useful if the Prosecution could state on the record which of those sessions and which documents it now seeks to have reclassified as public documents, and then the Chamber can order the Registry to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have -- I know we communicated the precise page references and the documents as well. I don't have that in front of me. I'll take the next opportunity to do so if the Court will permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's one way. The other way of dealing with it is to -- is for me to tell you what information the Tribunal has as to that. 11379, lines 19; 11380, line 14; 11401, line 20; 11405, line 4; and 11889 to 11895. And then the following portions should continue to be confidential under Rule 70: 11377 to 11379, line 18; 11380, line 15 to 11381; 11383 to 11395; 11397 to 11401, line 2; 11405, line 5 to 11406, line 1. And 11834 to 11838.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be, just for the transcript, 11834 to 11838.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the document is P2269.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And if the Prosecution is content with that information, then the Chamber will order the Registry to have those reclassified as public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: To make it plain, that extends to the audiovisual record as well. Any observations, Mr. Robinson, as to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I question why any of the material has to continue to remain protected under Rule 70. I think our arguments that were made also ought to be part of the public record given that there is now no reason whatsoever to have those materials be confidential. So it's our request that all of those pages be released to the public, not simply the testimony, but the argument about that too. I think it's part of -- it's important that the public record be clear. When pages are released later, only the most fanatic aficionados of this trial will actually read them when -- and the information that would otherwise have been public to the majority of the people who are watching the proceedings during the testimony of the witness will be lost, and so when we are making something public after the fact, I think it's important to -- that it also include the arguments as to why it should have been private in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, you've heard that. Perhaps you can formulate a response and we'll deal with that later. In addition, there is a ruling the Chamber wishes to issue at this stage, referring to the Prosecution's supplemental submission request concerning the Trial Chamber's order in relation to outstanding exhibit issues, Witness KDZ289 filed on 7 March 2011, which requested the Chamber to admit into evidence the public and under seal versions of the statements of Witness KDZ289 now that the required attestation as under Rule 92 bis(B) has been provided. Having reviewed KDZ289's certified statements, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the certification procedure fulfils the formal requirements of Rule 92 bis(B). The Chamber therefore requests the Registry to record that the confidential version of KDZ289 witness statement is admitted into evidence under seal as Exhibit P486. The Chamber also requests the Registry to assign an exhibit number to the document with Rule 65 ter number 90140A, which is the public version of KDZ289's witness statements, and to record that it is admitted into evidence. That being done, we should now continue to hear the witness's evidence. Mr. Prstojevic, I'm sorry that there has been a delay, but you will understand that there are administrative matters which crop up and have to be dealt with, but we are now in a position to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic. Can we call up --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up P960 very quickly, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, just before we adjourned the other day, we were looking at P960, the instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in emergency conditions dated 19 December 1991. And if we can turn to the next page, please, the document begins with a preamble indicating concerns that the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina will be taken out of Yugoslavia, and in light of the development of the overall political and security situation, goes on to identify tasks, measures and other activities to be implemented over the entire territory of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina in every municipality where the Serbian people live, and it's broken down into two variants, Variant A and B. And if we could turn to the next page, please. It's also broken down into two levels, as we see on the next page, Variant A first level, Variant B -- Variant A second level, Variant B first level and a Variant B second level. Turn to the first level, I'll indicate to you that the -- and you're free -- I'm sure you recall the document, but you're free to look to see whether the instructions for the first level for both Variant A and B are essentially the same. The first level, first instruction, is to introduce around-the-clock duty service in all SDS municipal boards and ensure constant communication and cooperation with all local boards on the territory of the municipality. Mr. Prstojevic, did you and the officials in Ilidza implement this provision of the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn quickly to point number 3, SDS municipal boards shall immediately establish Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in a municipality and then it goes on to explain aspects of the Crisis Staff's composition. Did you and the other officials in Ilidza establish a Crisis Staff pursuant to the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We established a Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza on the 2nd of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to the next page in English, point number 4, which -- that provides that the SDS local authorities shall convene and proclaim an Assembly of the Serbian People in the municipality composed of representatives of the Serbian people in the Municipal Assembly and so on. Did you and the officials in Ilidza convene and proclaim an Assembly of the Serbian People in the municipality pursuant to the fourth instruction in the body of the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We convened an Assembly of the Serbian People of Ilidza, made up of all SDS reformist and SDP [Realtime transcript read in error "SDA"] deputies. The majority of them were in attendance and then on the 3rd of January, 1992, we formed an Assembly of the Serbian People of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Call up 65 ter 14399, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The transcript reads "SDA" and the witness said "SDP."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, 65 ter 14399 is a document dated January 3rd, 1992. And it states, pursuant to the Article 265 of the constitution of SRBiH and the will of Serb people of Ilidza municipality expressed at a plebiscite held on 9 and 10 November 1991, and in accordance with the instruction by Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina main committee, number 079, dated 19 December 1991, the Assembly of Serb People of Ilidza at the session dated January 3rd, 1992, has rendered the following decision on proclaiming Serb Municipal Assembly of Ilidza. Do you recognise that document, Mr. Prstojevic, and is that the formalisation of the implementation of step number 4 or item number 4 in the December 19th, 1991, instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise it. This is our decision. So formally, from all Serb deputies, together with all the others, we established and proclaimed an Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. That was publicised immediately within the next few days because that was a public act and a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you notify the Bosnian Serb leadership that Ilidza had implemented this step?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that our administration department, as a rule, should have done that. Mr. Momcilo Ceklic, the secretary of the Assembly, should have forwarded this document to the relevant organs of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily to the president of the National Assembly of the Serbian people of B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we turn to the next page of the document, please? Sorry, and one more page beyond that, to the last page actually. And also in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we just have the one page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be a slight technological glitch but let me see if we can come up with that. Meanwhile, I will read to the witness what is contained in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, at the very end of the document, after it states that this decision shall enter into force immediately and shall be published in "Javnost," a Serb people paper, and then it's stamped and signed by the president of the Assembly, it indicates the following: "Submitted to," and that's the portion that is shown in English on the page, "Serb Assembly of BIH, for the attention of the president. SDS BiH, for the attention of the president. SDS BiH main committee, for the attention of the president. SDS main committee, for the attention of the president." And so on, naming some local officials. Is that consistent with your understanding that the implementation of item 4, at the first level for the instructions, was brought -- was reported to the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is stated in the document who the recipients are in the Serbian language, that is what the administration exactly did, and they made it -- mailed it through regular post. However, I have to underline that when establishing a Crisis Staff, we immediately deviated from this instruction by not strictly abiding by it. It was not convenient for us to have a document appointing the president of the -- the commander of the Crisis Staff in advance. The commander of the Crisis Staff was, rather, elected by the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the officials in Ilidza, yourself included, consider it your obligation to deliver to the Bosnian Serb leadership this document reflecting your implementation of the instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, we should have passed on this document to the relevant bodies of the Serbian people in the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prstojevic, you indicated a moment ago that -- let me find that. Before I move on I wanted to ask you one more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 1619, and before we do it, Your Honour, I would tender 14399.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P2408.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was 16199.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you see before you now, or you should see before you now, a document dated 3 January 1992, from the Assembly of Serbian Municipality Ilidza, stating that the Serb Assembly of the Ilidza municipality in its first session held on 3 January 1992, based on its received authorisations and the obvious necessity made the proposal of the decision. And it goes on to describe -- to start an initiative on the regulation of the status of Serb volunteers, their family members and the members of the Territorial Defence units, to make and adopt a decision regarding men of military age, and to immediately take the appropriate measures for the protection of the interests of the Serbian people in the territory of Ilidza, including protection of work organisations, institutions, et cetera. And it indicates that the decision has been forwarded to the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina for further realisation, and like the document we saw before, it was delivered to the president of the Serbian Assembly, the president of the SDS, the president of the Main Board, and so on. Mr. Prstojevic, do you recognise this document and is this one of the first decisions taken by the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality in Ilidza after its establishment pursuant to the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it, but this is not a decision. This is a proposal for a decision taken at our first session, to the effect that we are proposing to the Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina three things. Therefore, we were not authorised to pass this kind of decision but, rather, to make proposals only, and that was up to the Serbian Assembly of BiH to either accept or reject it. It was not up to us to decide. And from this decision, you can see who it was forwarded to and it was forwarded exclusively to the Serbian Assembly of BH, and you can see that because number 1 is the only one encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit P2409.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you indicated a few moments ago that officials in the -- the SDS officials in Ilidza established a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the composition of that Crisis Staff, Mr. Prstojevic? Who was in it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we didn't automatically act according to the instructions. At the municipal council, I wanted a democratically elected commander of the Crisis Staff, which was not in accordance with the instructions, and the Crisis Staff elected me as the commander of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff comprised municipal functionaries who worked at the Ilidza municipality, the people's deputy, the commander of the TO staff, and representatives of the local Crisis Staffs. I would like to emphasise that by forming the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Ilidza and by establishing the Assembly, we completed the instructions. The functionaries who worked at the Ilidza municipality and I myself continued to work normally in the joint Assembly of the municipality of Ilidza, and we would not do anything else in accordance with the agreement until the beginning of the war in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the top Serbian police official in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim Edin Mlivic was head of the police. He was chief of the public security station. The number 2 man was a Serb, commander of the police station, that was Mr. Tomo Kovac, and according to the functional principle, he was also a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Ilidza accountable to the state and political bodies that issued the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we completed this formal part, and that until the beginning of the war we didn't do anything, and we were not responsible to anyone for anything. There was no action and there was no responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, do you recall that during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you were asked about subordination and accountability of the Serbian Crisis Staff in Ilidza, and would it refresh your recollection about accountability if I indicated what that exchange consisted of? You said the following at page 14619: "The Crisis Staff at Ilidza was basically set up and operated in line with the instructions that I saw here. And I've referred in the interview 093, I believe, 093, it is quite clear that the responsibility of the Crisis Staff had to do with the fact that they were accountable to the state and political bodies that issued those instructions and asked for them to be implemented. Basically, coordinating activities of the Crisis Staff would be subject to consultations and agreement with the top political and state leadership." Now, first of all, Mr. Prstojevic, that's -- and do you agree that's what you said during the course of the Krajisnik case, under oath?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's exactly what I'm saying. We founded the Crisis Staff pursuant to the instructions with the change that the municipal board would be electing the commander of the Crisis Staff. We established the Assembly. So we completed that formal part, and informed the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And thereby, we felt that we had done our part of the job responsibly, in a responsible way. We published that it and this was published by the Bosnian and Herzegovinian press. Then we didn't have any other activities. We were not warned by anyone about having to do anything either. Thus, the formal hierarchy exists. Above the Ilidza Assembly is the Assembly of the Serbian People of BiH but we didn't do anything, and I don't have any evidence or any documents of anyone from the leadership of the Serbian people warning us about anything or about us having to report back about anything. I am not disputing the hierarchy at all. It exists in all countries, all states.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff established at the beginning of January 1992 continued to exist into April and May 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was established, as I said, and it didn't do anything until the 3rd of April, 1992. On the 10th of April, 1992, a new Crisis Staff would be established in line with the new Assembly that had nothing to do with this instructions. From the 5th of April, 1992, and that will be the basis of continued work. Practically all my wartime activities and work of the functionaries, the commanders of the TO staff and the civilian protection in Ilidza was determined by the war and the new Assembly from the 5th of April, 1992, that numbered 70 deputies, and that issued the authority to the president of the Assembly to form the Crisis Staff and in the -- and gave him unlimited authority in the imminent threat of war time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A few moments ago you described the composition of the Crisis Staff established in January of 1992. What do you claim was the difference between the composition of the Crisis Staff established on the 10th of April and the Crisis Staff that had existed up to that time? For example, did you continue as president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's not fair to the witness. He said that that was the party Crisis Staff and this one was the municipal Crisis Staff. The municipal -- the municipal staff is an organ of the government, whereas the other one is a party organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should be cross-examining both the accused and Mr. Prstojevic on this subject. I think I made a distinction between the two that was perfectly fair and allowed the witness to answer the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that was my view. Mr. Witness, can you deal with that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Prstojevic. A few moments ago you described the composition of the Crisis Staff established in January of 1992. What do you claim was the difference between the composition of the Crisis Staff established on the 10th of April and the Crisis Staff that had existed up to that time? For example, did you continue as president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is in the fact that there I was elected by the municipal board, and that was in line with the instructions. The second time that I was appointed commander of the Crisis Staff, it was because the Assembly of the 5th of April declared an imminent threat of war to the Serbian people in Ilidza because the Muslim leadership had already proclaimed, on the 5th of April, a general mobilisation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a general mobilisation of the units of the Territorial Defence, units of the MUP, units of the civilian protection, and the confiscation, the seizing, the robbing of weapons from the JNA and from the MUP. This was practically a declaration of war in relation to the Serbs and the Croats, and that is why our Assembly, already the following day, as soon as we heard this, proclaimed the imminent danger of war, imminent threat of war, and gave unlimited powers to the president of the Assembly to form a new Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, with respect, I think now that you have essentially both repeated and elaborated on the accused's objection, I would ask you to answer my question which was about the composition of the staff. Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the Crisis Staff of the 10th of April was completely different from the previous one. There are a lot of new people there but the functional connection was still maintained, meaning that some functionaries from the MUP and the Territorial Defence were in it. That composition of the Crisis Staff was more numerous, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were still president; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out the function of the president from the 5th of April, 1992. Up until then I was the secretary for inspection of the Municipal Assembly of the -- of Ilidza, and my last day at that post was the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence, the Serbian Territorial Defence, Mr. Markovic, was still a member of the Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, the commander of the police and the leading Serbian official in the MUP was still a member of the Crisis Staff and attended meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a bit about subordination and you've talked about the functional connection and the hierarchy as it -- and referred to hierarchy that you compared to all other states. Let me ask you what body and what person was at the top of the hierarchy of the -- of, first, the Serbian authorities before April and then after April?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, the top political organ was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where our representatives, Madam Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Professor Nikola Koljevic, were a part of it. That was the top leadership. After the war began, I don't know the exact date, when the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, the highest body again would be, when it was formed, the Presidency of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the president of the Assembly and the government were the other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the pre-eminent leader of the SDS? Who was the top leader of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, and after the war, the president of our party was Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to the time when, in April, when the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina began not to function with respect to the Serbian people, and the organs of Republika Srpska were being formed, who did you consider to be the leadership of that new entity and of the SDS? And again going from the top down, whether elected or not. Who were they, in order?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say here that for some 15 days or more, we didn't even know what was going on with the leadership of the Serbian people. Madam Biljana Plavsic was in Sarajevo, held as a hostage. We didn't know if President Karadzic was alive. We didn't know where Nikola Koljevic was. We simply didn't know what was happening to anyone for the first 15 days or longer. The key decisive part of the beginning of the war, as far as Ilidza was concerned, meant that we were working on our own during that time. And only around the 20th of April, we would find out that President Karadzic was alive, we would see some members of the government, and the Prime Minister, the president of the Assembly, and so on and so forth, and I don't know -- I already said that -- I didn't know when the Presidency would be formed, and exactly when that happened, because we didn't follow that. The wartime situation didn't permit us to do that. We were simply doing what we had to do in order to protect our people from suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let me see if I can't refresh your recollection about something you indicated in the -- during the course of the Karadzic [sic] case was perfectly clear. At page 14566, you were asked by Judge Orie, with respect to the period in 1992: "... when the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not function well anymore and the Serbian Assembly and later Republika Srpska was established. Who did you consider to be the leadership of that new entity, and of the SDS? Please, from the top going further down. Whether they were elected or not, that's another matter. Just name them from the top down." And you said: "That is perfectly clear. Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Mr. Momo Krajisnik, Prime Minister Djeric, ministers of internal affairs and the Minister of Justice." Now, that's what you said under oath in 2005, correct, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, but that refers to this period, from the time we found out -- when we saw the leadership all together, assembled in Ilidza. Up until that time, the situation was chaotic, and I even made a mistake there. At the time, around the 20th of April, I think that the Prime Minister was Miodrag Simovic. It wasn't Djeric, actually. Djeric came later, which also indicates that I was thinking about this period when the Pale government began to operate because on the 18th of April, the president, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the president of the Assembly, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, about eight members of the government, the president -- the Prime Minister Simovic, would come to Ilidza and that is where they discussed where the seat of the government would be. The decision was not made at the time, but we were told that we would be told where the government would be located. After that, on the 18th of April, I don't know, maybe in five or six days or more, it was reported that the government would be located at Pale and that the Prime Minister remained in Sarajevo because he couldn't get out of the Muslim part of Sarajevo. And that's when that hierarchy began to function. It's not something that I'm disputing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, a couple of things, Mr. Prstojevic. First of all, are you aware that Mr. Djeric was elected the president of the government, that is the Prime Minister, at a session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on -- on or about March 24th, 1992, about a month before the period -- the date that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Secondly, you referred to a meeting on or about the 18th of April in Ilidza, involving Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik and others, to discuss where the seat of the government would be. Is it correct that that was a meeting to discuss the political and military situation and one of the topics was where the seat of the government would be?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but it is not correct, what you say. What is correct is that the meeting was exclusively held to see where the seat of the government would be. It's correct that there was a vote in the government, four to four. Part were in favour of the government being in Ilidza, and the other part was for the government to be located outside of Ilidza. So it was half and half. The meeting was chaired by Simovic, Miodrag Simovic. At the meeting, I, as the president of the municipality, as well as five or six of my men who attended that meeting, felt it was necessary for us to inform our leadership about the military-security situation, meaning we are ruling out the political situation because from the beginning of the war, we did not have any political actions, and neither did we divide the people according to which party they belonged to. It was our initiative to inform the leadership in a way that is the proper thing to do, in the introductory part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will be talking about that meeting later in your examination, Mr. Prstojevic, so I will defer any further questions about that for the moment. Let me turn -- let me continue, however, talking about the nature of the institutions in Serbian Ilidza, and the hierarchy and subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, if I could call up 65 ter 00575.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Prstojevic, is dated 16 April 1992. It's a document from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of National Defence, and it's pursuant to Articles of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH, and it's a decision that a Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be formed. First of all, do you recognise that document, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise this document. However, I can see what it contains. Therefore, I assume that this is an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's continue to the last page. It bears the name of Bogdan Subotic as Minister of Defence, and there is a stamp from the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. First of all, you recall that Bogdan Subotic was the Minister of Defence of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did -- what effect did -- if any, did this decision have on the Territorial Defence in Serbian Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision, as far as the territory of the Serbian Ilidza is concerned, produced a consequence in terms that we knew that the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian people of B and H had become operative, that it's starting working, and that in a way a structure was being put in place of hierarchical TO defence units. Secondly, and I have to underline this, this decision relating to Ilidza was rather belated. If we hadn't done what we had, I would not have survived. We -- actually not we, but I personally, pursuant to the authority of the Assembly, I declared a general mobilisation on the 6th of April, and I have with me the original of this decision, which is very illustrative of how we worked. That was the first decision that I took based on the authority vested in me by the Assembly. And I already said that on the 5th we already declared an imminent threat of war. In other words, for the whole 10 days we were ahead of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. I can produce this decision with the original stamp and my original signature, and it is a very indicative decision. It was forwarded to the Crisis Staff, the Secretariat for National Defence, to the Ilidza Public Security Station, and it was put on a public board. Therefore, it was placed in the public domain and it was also kept in archives. Not a single document that either I or the Crisis Staff adopted were -- was a strictly confidential one. Our intention was for us to operate in open so that all citizens, regardless of their ethnicity, would know what we were doing. And I would gladly present this decision to this honourable Chamber in order to inspect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please provide that to the Registry, Mr. Prstojevic, and we'll have that marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I should have asked for the Court's permission but I thought that would be the manner in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If the witness is volunteering a useful document then, of course, that should be provided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P2410, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, did the 16 April decision by Subotic essentially approve and formalise what Ilidza had already implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. It cannot formalise anything retroactively. However, from that moment on, the TO staff of the Serbian Republic of BH was set up, as well as municipal TO staffs that were part of the whole hierarchy, and hierarchical links. It has nothing to do with what we had done before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can explain something, then, in -- during the course of the Krajisnik case at page 14541. You were talking about this decision and you said: "In Ilidza, the units of the Territorial Defence had been mobilised earlier because the formal official in charge of Ilidza before the war was in his proper position and everything functioned well, and the decision that came only sort of approved and formalised the -- what we had already implemented on the ground, and approved that our steps to prepare the defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were correct." First of all, is that what you stated under oath in the Krajisnik case and was that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How I formulate that in the Krajisnik case is something that I would like to hear from the CD. It is sure that in your translations from Serbian into English, there is a huge number of mistakes. Or if a word is translated in a different manner, it can alter its meaning. I would like to say, although reluctantly, that some of the interpreters during my interviews left out entire portions of my statements when translating, and I don't understand that a document can verify anything retroactively. However, it is true that the TO Staff Commander was Dragan Markovic, a Serb, but he was not a member of the SDS. He was a Serb, though, and it made our job easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you consider, Mr. Prstojevic, that the appointment of General Subotic as the republic-level Minister of Defence signalled the establishment of the hierarchy of the TO in -- for the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall that that took place -- do you recall when that took place?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, that was in the third decade -- in the third part of April. It wasn't on the 16th. God knows when we received it. Never mind, we did receive it, but it could not have arrived on the 17th. It could have arrived only from the 18th onwards, inclusive the 18th, because, quite simply, at that time the postal service was not operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in 2005, you were fairly emphatic about a particular date, and let me read you your testimony at page 14542. You said, then, when you were asked about the chain of command of the Serbian Territorial Defence, from Ilidza up to the top level of command, you said -- and that was a question by the Judge, you said: "Up to the 10th -- up to the 11th of April, 1992, the chain of command did not exist. What existed were only advisory meetings and briefings. Did I say 11th of April, 1992? Yes. From the 11th April on, when General Subotic was appointed Minister of Defence, consultations with the Ministry of Defence and the minister himself began, and from that point on, the hierarchy was established." Is -- again, Mr. Prstojevic, is that what you said under oath during the course of the Krajisnik case and was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that my memory was better at the time, or that I knew the date when Minister Subotic came out publicly with his statement of the 11th of April, and if I said that, then it is correct. As for this document, what I'm saying now is also correct. It was dated the 16th at -- and it took at least two days for the postal service to deliver it. Therefore, I stand by my evidence in the Krajisnik case, and the evidence given here. They are simply complementary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, sitting schedule today is that we are going to sit until 1.45. I propose we take a break now for 30 minutes until 10.45. We will sit again and then -- until 12, break until 12.30 and then continue on till 13.45, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm in the Court's hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We will rise now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before Mr. Tieger resumes I wonder if I could just raise one point with respect to the nature of this examination. In some instances, Mr. Tieger has been putting to the witness testimony that he gave in the Krajisnik case. In particular, I call your attention to a paragraph 23 of the transcript, when he elicited that the witness had said that from the 11th of April on, when General Subotic was appointed as Minister of Defence, consultations with the Ministry of the Defence and the minister himself began and from that point on the hierarchy was established. That was the portion that Mr. Tieger read out. But in the same transcript, a few lines later, the witness had said: "However, if you allow me one more thing, from that date, the 16th of April until the 19th of May, when the Army of Republika Srpska was created, for the most part, in the area of Ilidza municipality, our staff of Territorial Defence organised our defence on its own initiative, with the verbal support and minimal, almost symbolic logistical support from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska." So we don't feel that in that instance the whole passage was actually read to the witness, which would have been more fair since the witness himself doesn't have access to the transcript and isn't able to raise those issues himself. Secondly, in the Popovic appeals decision of the 1st of February, 2008, entitled, "Decision on appeals against decision on impeachment of a party's own witness," in paragraph 26 it indicates that it should be the Trial Chamber who decides -- or the parties should apply for permission from the Trial Chamber when it is going to embark upon impeaching its own witness. And it's unclear from the way Mr. Tieger is doing it whether he's genuinely trying to refresh the witness's recollection or whether he's actually using the testimony to impeach the witness. And I think that he ought to be -- when he's using it for impeachment, he ought to be making -- asking for permission from the Trial Chamber before doing that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Your Honour, I think these kinds of discussions should take place outside the presence of the witness. If Mr. Robinson knew he was going to raise it, as I assume he did, he should have alerted the Chamber's officials. If we are going to continue this, and I think the Court wants a response, I understand the witness does not understand English, he may be able to remove his headphones. I want to say before he does, however, that I'm -- one of the things I'm going to say that is that the passage that was read by Mr. Robinson was not precisely relevant to the point I was asking the witness about, and I don't want the witness to be -- to have it suggested to the witness that I'm misleading him by asking -- by quoting him portions of the transcript out of context. But to continue the discussion, I think that should be either outside the presence of the witness, either physically or with his earphones off, if that -- if that means he's effectively not participating in procedural discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm simply wondering at the moment whether it's necessary at all, Mr. Tieger. There are two aspects to this, it seems to me. First of all, if the Defence have a valid point, that's a point that can be put to the witness and emphasised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Secondly, and I speak just for myself at the moment, I wasn't under the impression myself that you were seeking to impeach the witness, and obviously, if that position came to pass, no doubt you would make it plain to the parties that that was your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated earlier that in the course of a -- another discussion, but a related discussion, that there can sometimes be -- that -- in the course of illuminating to the extent possible the information that a witness may be able to provide the Chamber, that may occur in the context of what is normally viewed as refreshing recollection, it may occur in the context of what may be seen as impeachment and so on. For that reason I raised all of those possibilities with the Court earlier so that the Court was aware of -- and indeed also the manner in which we would proceed in this fashion with open-ended questions to the extent possible, proceeding toward a focus on particular passages that might further illuminate the issues involved. That's what I'm attempting to do. I don't understand from either the Popovic case or the practice of this Chamber or the practice in other cases that that entails a moment-by-moment request for permission to delve into prior statements, and it would be quite -- I think -- unnecessarily awkward and inefficient if we were to do that. I think the manner in which we have been proceeding is entirely fair. The Court can follow it, as can the Defence, and I don't think it's involved any burdens or difficulties that warrant a change in the approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, you've made your point, and it's a point that is proper to make, but I think we can continue effectively, if perhaps robustly, without a constant intervention as to seeking permission to impeach, unless and until there is a radical impeachment that falls entirely outside the concept or scope of aide-memoire. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, just before we adjourned, I had been asking you some questions about the Territorial Defence, and let me ask you this: When the VRS was formed, the Army of Republika Srpska, did the TO of Ilidza then merge into the VRS, the VRS units?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, practically Territorial Defence units were the Army of Republika Srpska. That was one and the same thing. There was no segment outside of the Territorial Defence. You are asking me whether they merged as if those were two separate entities. TO ceased practically to be a TO, and it became Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also mentioned earlier the Serbian -- the MUP, at least you mentioned a MUP official and the existence of the MUP in Ilidza. Was a Serbian MUP formed in Ilidza and when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP is another entity or a component which is solely dealing with the safety of citizens, the protection of the citizens and territory and public law and order. According to what I know, in compliance with agreements reached at the highest level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a division was agreed to be carried out on or around the 1st of April, throughout the republic, i.e. in Sarajevo. In practical terms, this division was to take place between the 3rd and -- between the 1st and 3rd April. In a way, this division was completed and the 3rd of April is the crucial date indicating that on that date the Serbs from the special base of Krte, which was the best special MUP base in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, abandoned it, and that was on a Friday, that was the last working day of that week, and they had never returned since. And from that point on the MUPs started operating independently. In other words, after the 3rd of April, the MUPs, the Muslim one, the Serbian one, and later on the Croatian one, started operating independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the Serbian MUP in Ilidza, after its creation, subordinated to the republic level of the authorities of Republika Srpska or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are hierarchical links between the MUP and the government of Republika Srpska, and it is subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And ultimately, was the president of the republic or the Presidency at the very top of the hierarchy in Republika Srpska? That is the highest body and the highest official?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's self-explanatory, i.e., that the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH was the highest authority in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we've been focusing over the last few minutes on the period of April or so, with some reference to May as well. Let me ask you whether, in April and May of 1992, and even later, there were also paramilitary groups in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain groups that could be considered paramilitary groups. However, I have to explain here that by mobilisation rules, the territorial -- of the Territorial Defence imply the volunteer principle of incorporating volunteers, groups or individuals into the TO units and later into the Army of Republika Srpska or the MUP. And in that sense, the volunteers would be coming individually, from all Serbian lands, as well as Serbs from America, from Canada, from the European Union countries. If organised or self-organised groups were arriving, they would, at some point, tend to exhibit some disobedience, regardless of whether they were part of the MUP or of the military, and there were also from our local units of the Serbian army, that would at a certain point in time try to be more independent of the command, especially in logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let's begin by having you tell the Court who some of these paramilitary groups were. Whether you call them paramilitary groups or volunteer groups. First of all, was there a group associated with Mr. Seselj's party?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically how linked they were because if a group came, they would introduce themselves. They would have to report to Ilidza. When the Crisis Staff was there they would have to report to the Crisis Staff. Later they would have to report to the brigade command or the MUP. Sometimes we could receive them all, myself, the commander of the brigade, the chief of the MUP. I don't know if they belonged to Seselj or not. It's very difficult to establish that because the Radical Party in Ilidza was founded, I think, sometime in June or July, July 1992. I do have that piece of information but I don't have it with me, because it was registered in Ilidza. But I am aware that they said that they belonged to the Radical Party. Our local unit, the unit of Gavrilovic, Brne, mostly it was that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to saying that they belonged to the Radical Party, were they visited by Mr. Seselj himself? And did he tour their positions?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj visited the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza on one occasion. Before that, he toured a unit that was made up of local Serbs from the area of Sarajevo. It was the unit of Brne Gavrilovic, and the visit really provided just moral support, psychological support. That's all we had from it. But I'm not aware that Mr. Seselj got ready a single truck of humanitarian aid for Ilidza. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how many times did Mr. Seselj visit Brne's group and did that indicate the extent to which they were connected?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj came to Ilidza twice. The first time I received him, he came to the Municipal Assembly building, and the second time, since the Radical Party had already taken root in Ilidza during the war, it started its struggle for power before we started with our party activities or paying attention to who was in what party, he didn't even deign to come and visit me at my office at the Municipal Assembly of Serbian Ilidza. He was more busy with promoting the Serbian Radical Party, using his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And visiting Brne's group, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were Arkanovci, that is forces of Zeljko Raznatovic, also known as Arkan, in Ilidza in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's group did not come to Ilidza in April. According to what I know, Arkan never came to Ilidza. However, a smaller group of his men came to Ilidza on the 12th of May, when we had quite intense fighting on that day, on the south-western front. The group stayed there on the 12th, the 13th, which was a quiet day. They arrived on the 12th in the evening. On the 13th, they came to see me. They visited me at the Crisis Staff. They were interested about the organisation, the defence lines, mostly in the military and security situation. On the 14th of May, we had a horrendous attack on Ilidza by Muslim forces, at the interior and the exterior defence ring, stretching for some 30 kilometres of the front. That day they took part in defensive actions. You could say that they fought exceptionally well. But for some reasons unknown to me, they left our territory immediately after the 14th of May. Perhaps it was the 15th or the 16th of May. I don't know. Because the fighting was intense that day, they had I don't know how many wounded, perhaps that was also one reason for their withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me quickly call up 65 ter 3075 -- excuse me, P2229.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, that's an intercepted telephone conversation involving Mico Stanisic and Nedjeljko Zugic. It's relatively brief so I ask you to look at that. Mr. Stanisic -- and it's dated 15 May 1992. Mr. Stanisic indicating the Serb MUP is calling, and some exchanges. Then towards the bottom of the page in English and also in Serbian, Zugic indicates he's in the Serb Municipality of Ilidza with Vuk, Mlaco, Prstojevic. And if we turn the page, please. Stanisic wants to know what the situation is like. Zugic says, We have got reinforcements from Gagovic, some Arkanovci and Seseljevci came. And Stanisic says, Good. And is that a further reflection of the presence of Arkanovci and Seseljevci in Ilidza at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment these conversations just based on the text alone. The date does coincide with the date that I said they were there. As for the other names that Zugic mentions, I don't know them. I don't know if these are people from Arkan's unit or from some other unit. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, do you recall that at that time, you yourself -- first of all, let me ask you who was Mr. Gagovic who is referred to in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gagovic is one of the assistant commanders from the JNA army. That was still the JNA at the time. However, it's incorrect that we got any help from Gagovic at the time because, as a rule, he was the one who needed help. Perhaps it was technical assistance, but as far as the manpower is concerned, we were the ones who were protecting the JNA barracks in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were in contact with Mr. Gagovic during that period of time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the day before do you recall that you were speaking with Mr. Gagovic about, among other things, Arkanovci?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did. The fighting was going on, and the Arkan's men were participating, so probably, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's look quickly at 65 ter 31679.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, this is a conversation that you listened to previously at least once and perhaps more. So I'll ask to you read it quickly and I'll direct your attention to certain portions.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have something to say here. All intercepted telephone conversations provided to you by AID, either are not original or the most original. Why? In the conversations that I listened to, when I use a strong word, it can be heard very clearly, and when I am speaking about something humane, warmer, that is quieter, less audible. Secondly, when the interpreters or translators translate that same conversation, telephone conversation, into English, they often change a word or use a word that changes the meaning, or they drop some text, they put three dots, they say "unclear." Even here you can see such examples, in three places that I can see with three dots in one second. So I would prefer to hear the original of the conversation, of this intercepted conversation, so that I could establish the differences from the original and the transcribed text and point them out. That is my general position towards all documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, I'm going to leave this to the Court but let me point out that this -- see if you recall that, among other things, you heard the entirety of this conversation during the course of the Krajisnik case and you had heard it earlier as well, as you indicated to the Court at that time, at page 14557. You indicated that you didn't recall the conversation but listening to your own voice and: "... listening to Gagovic's voice and trying to place it all within the context of the military situation at the time, which is quite clear to me, well, of course, I can admit to having participated in this conversation. So obviously I was at Ilidza and Lieutenant Gagovic from the corps command at Lukavica." Now I'm going to direct your attention to particular portions. If you then want to hear the audio of the conversation, we can do that, but you may be able to answer the question without recourse to the particular audio. And further, Mr. Prstojevic, let me tell you that these conversations are transcribed in Serbian from the audio. Now, if we could turn the page, please -- well, first of all before we do, let me -- there is -- towards the bottom of page 1, the conversation reflects you complaining about hardware and Gagovic replying about someone who has manpower but not hardware, et cetera. So that's a bit of the subject. At the end you say: "Popadic is there on the terrain, at the spot. At least two vehicles, two armoured personnel carriers should be replaced at this check-point." And if we could turn the page, there is further conversations, Gagovic asks: "Are the APCs that arrived yesterday all right?" You say: "Yes, the ones that arrived yesterday." He asks if there is a tank in working order and you should pull out the APCs. You respond you're not sure if anything is in working order, two tanks, three APCs and so on. Gagovic curses. And you say: "And those two yesterday are with Arkan's men." Mr. Prstojevic, do you have any reason to doubt that the passage in which you're referring to the APCs being with -- or to the hardware being with Arkan's men is a transcription error or does it refer to the presence of Arkan's forces in Ilidza and your awareness of that and working with them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I accept what I said earlier, because generally, I really don't recall the conversation, but when I recognise my voice and the voice of my collocutor and knowing the military situation, the wartime situation at the time, then I can explain. However, it's correct that it the AID has been providing to you copies of telephone conversations and that in this conversation, in a number of places, what I said has not been translated in its entirety. Secondly I do not dispute in this conversation anything what I said before and I can explain what I said before, but you just need to put specific questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did. Does this accurately reflect the presence of Arkan's forces in Ilidza and your awareness of that and you're working with them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I received Arkan's men, headed by Legija, on the 13th at the Crisis Staff. On the 14th of May, at 5.08, when the attack on Ilidza began, at the front, some 30 kilometres, these men were also participating in the fighting at a specific sector of the front, and it's not in dispute that they also had some of their own hardware and that, in battle, if they knew how to handle an APC, they would then take it and use it in the fighting and in the defence. That's what happened ultimately, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was left out of this conversation, Mr. Prstojevic, that you want to tell us about, if anything?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know that, but if you let me see the beginning again I'm going to tell you where three dots appear. One, two, three, fourth line from the bottom, there are some things missing. Sixth line from the bottom, three dots, something is missing because three dots in the Serbian language means that something more is being said. Also the fourth or the fifth row from the top, again you see three dots. Again something is left out. So you cannot really get a true picture of the conversation. This conversation is not that important but there are some that are important. There is practically nothing of dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good. And we will listen to some telephone conversations, Mr. Prstojevic, but you should be cautious about interpreting these transcriptions. You've had a chance to hear the intercepts, correct? Many of the intercepts? Just "yes" or "no," please, because I want to ask a question after that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes, but at that point in time, I didn't have this text in front of me to be able to compare, to say, for example, in line 5, they dropped this and this and this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to hear that people talking on the telephone often interrupt each other or talk over each other and that's what you see three lines representing, when a person speaking concludes that portion, another person picks up, and the transcribers can't capture the entirety of that conversation. You've noticed that, haven't you, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Three dots in the Serbian language means that the speaker said something else. Where two conversations are overlapping, then this guy here would mark "unclear" or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Maybe just my eyesight but in the fifth line from the bottom, I perceive it's four dots, not three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not aware that that is an intended distinction, unless it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the only reason I mention it is the witness was very specific about what three dots meant. There may be nothing in it but there may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prstojevic, can you respond to the Court? Do you have a view on what four dots mean instead of three?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They practically mean the same thing, and perhaps indicate even more words than three dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court will have the audios and we will be hearing some other audios as well, Mr. Prstojevic. Were there -- besides Brne's group and Arkan's group, were there other paramilitary groups that arrived in Ilidza in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say this: In April, there were no outside groups, none. Brne came in June -- actually, in July. He came and he was within the MUP contingent. The Arkan people came when I already mentioned. Later during the year, a Zvornik unit appeared from Zvornik from Republika Srpska. They referred to it also as Zvornik Chetniks. I noticed that group in December. At one point, there was a group belonging to some Bokan, also numbering some 15 men. These are small formations. This group was billeted -- well, all of them had to be included either in a MUP or in the army. When it was placed within one of these forces, it didn't take part either in the fighting or the defence because there were no attacks at that particular time. And then they returned wherever they came from. As time went along, Ilidza got quite organised, everything was functioning, and all the personnel had to be placed under the command of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska. The brigades. And only at the beginning, at one point in time, Brne's group was in the MUP, but then later, at the end of the year, it became part of the Igman Brigade. And these things that I'm saying, I have written documents about that. I have them here. I have the conclusion from the second session of the Ilidza Municipal Assembly from 1992, which literally states that each individual, each group, must be part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to P2302, please? And Your Honour, may the previous intercept be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness did say there was nothing in there which he contested, so yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2411, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, am I right in thinking that intercepts are being admitted as MFI'd documents? Or have we changed this practice without me noticing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but under the guidelines when a participant recognises the intercept, that is not MFI'd but admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that was the view I took. Certainly aware the witness can't -- the witness is saying that it's not, in his recollection, complete, but that part of it which is there he accepts as being accurate. In that case, there is nothing to MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So I think that answers your question, Dr. Karadzic. It's only where there is a disputed part of the text in terms of the text which is there that it's necessary to MFI it. It's always open to add to the document, if indeed there are omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We certainly have had intercepts where there is nothing in particular disputed, but where, in line with the protocol, the witness is not a participant, then they have been MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, there must be a distinction drawn between those intercepts where the witness is a participant and those that aren't, but I'm grateful for you drawing it to my attention, Dr. Karadzic, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the document before you now is an approval dated July 9th, 1992, from the war board of commissioners, Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, and it bears your name and a signature and a stamp. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it is an approval for Branislav Gavrilovic, the commander of all SAO Romanija volunteer units, to conduct the admission and training of Serbian volunteers using the motel facility in Gladno Polje. First of all, is -- I think you've mentioned his full name, but Branislav Gavrilovic is the Brne you've been talking about before, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is this a reflection of Brne's subordination to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you have referred during the course of your testimony to meetings and consultations, sometimes to specific ones, sometimes more generally, and I'd like to ask you some questions about at least a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain this approval to a greater detail. If you permit me to explain how this particular premises were allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- first of all, Mr. Prstojevic, a witness is indeed entitled to explain, but the mechanics of how the facility was allocated to Brne may not be of the utmost relevance to the Court at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think that's probably true. If you could simply answer Mr. Tieger's question at the moment, and if necessary, the explanation can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn to a topic, as I say, you've alluded to before, and that was meetings and consultations that took place between officials in Ilidza, including yourself, and the leadership of Republika Srpska. First of all, Mr. Prstojevic, let me turn your attention to the period just before April 1992. Do you recall that there was a meeting of a military/security nature toward the latter part of March 1992, that is before the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that meeting from other people's stories, specifically from two of our people who attended the meeting. I suppose that this meeting was held at the level of the city of Sarajevo. In that meeting, security and political situation was being discussed. They briefly informed me about what they had heard at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "other people," are you referring to other members of the Crisis Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to two officials from Ilidza municipality, i.e., the president of the Executive Committee of Ilidza municipality, and the TO Staff Commander of Ilidza municipality, and that was a period when we operated jointly, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- the president of the Executive Committee, was that Mr. Kezunovic, and the president of -- and the commander of the TO, that was Mr. Markovic, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radomir Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were they both --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were they both members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but the Crisis Staff was inactive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So they told you there had been a meeting of a military/security -- a security and political nature. What did they tell you was discussed at that meeting? Well, first of all, let me ask you who else was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know at which particular level this meeting was held, and who attended. Now, by analogy, since two officials from our municipality attended, I can only assume that people from other municipalities, holding similar offices, were in attendance as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the meeting also attended by people from the leadership of the party?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but if it was held at the city level, somebody should have been there, but as I said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the president of the Executive Committee or the commander of the TO tell you not only that people from the leadership of the party were present but also what the people from the leadership of the party had said?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I remember about this meeting is that in the portion of the meeting relating to the security situation, there were people of lower or middle range of ranking who were rather optimistic because they did not believe that the Serbian people were actually in danger as they were, and that if they came under attack, it would have been much easier to defend ourselves than we, in Ilidza, thought. And perhaps this situation might have prevailed in some of the municipalities. And they realised that these people are full of self-confidence and that they were, I won't like to say this, but that they were militant. However, our situation was completely different. It was a very difficult and uncertain one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you said that -- you just said you don't like to refer to it as such but it was militant. Was there threatening rhetoric used by persons at the meeting? And in particular, persons who were from the leadership of the party?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I don't know who said that and whether it was a commander of a staff from a municipality or someone from Sarajevo or someone completely different. All of this ended, all this exchange of information, over coffee. And now, in the year 2003 and later, somebody is asking me about this. I mentioned this and now it turns out that this was a critically important meeting, but it wasn't important at all because no specific tasks were passed on to us in Ilidza as a result of that meeting. Because, had that been the case, I would have remembered that very well and I would have known whether I would comply with that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Prstojevic, the people who were -- first of all, I didn't get an answer to my question, although you're free to offer clarifications when they are useful. Was there threatening rhetoric used at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by some people, but only under the scenario of us coming under an attack. If we became the subject of an aggressive move made by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wasn't it the case, Mr. Prstojevic, that that threatening rhetoric was about what would or should happen if there wasn't an agreement on the -- with the Bosnian Muslims, about the organisation or division of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not the case. Now, I will quote an original sentence that I heard from one of the two men that I mentioned earlier, and I apologise to everyone present in this courtroom. Somebody literally said the following: "If we fail to reach an agreement, if we are attacked, we are going to fuck their mothers." So this is this exaggerated self-confidence, not to qualify it as militancy. I don't know any harsher word than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at the time, Mr. Prstojevic, based on your discussions with the Ilidza representatives who were present, did you understand that to mean that there would essentially be division one way or another, either by -- in a peaceful manner or by force?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give it a thought. I realised if it comes to armed fighting, some people believed that would easily push back the Muslim forces and we didn't share their opinion, because war was in the air already. Everybody could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, let me turn your attention, if I may, to an interview you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in November of 2003, at a time closer to the events that we are discussing than now. That's 65 ter 07875. And I believe that's page 11 of the English and page 7 of the Serbian. And begin with the portion where you say: "At that meeting there was a lot of threatening rhetoric" -- well, first of all, to maybe orient you, Mr. Prstojevic, you say -- if you see the portion that says: "Sometime before the 1st of April," and that may be on the previous page in B/C/S for you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see it at the bottom of the page now? The bottom of the -- the bottom of the page where -- the very end of you speaking on that page.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the beginning that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to orient you before moving you on to the next page and indicate we are speaking that particular meeting. So where it says, [B/C/S spoken]. All right, and you give the date of the meeting. Now let's move to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I'm telling you all the time, that the Serbian and the English version do not correspond to each other. So the beginning is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was actually directing your attention to the bottom, not the beginning. All right. If you'll follow now at the top of the -- toward the top of the page you say the following: "I understood that at that meeting there was a lot of -- at that meeting there was a lot of threatening rhetoric.
